lesson.title: A reliable first program
lesson.example:
Input: 6
2 5 4 7 8 9

Python:
values = [2, 5, 4, 7, 8, 9]
count = 0
for index, value in enumerate(values):
    if index % 2 == value % 2:
        count += 1
print(count)  # 6
lesson.explanation: An index describes a position, not a value. Enumerate supplies both. The counter means: how many matching positions have been seen so far. Before the loop it is zero; each iteration changes it only when the condition holds. This gives a simple correctness argument. For submitted problems, replace the demonstration array with input parsing and print only the answer.
lesson.pitfall: Do not assume values are positive or use one-based positions when a prompt specifies zero-based indices.
lesson.checkpoint: Can you explain what the counter represents after the first three iterations? Test a one-element array and an array containing negative odd values.

lesson.title: Scan once, keep the right state
lesson.example:
String: abbcccde
Runs: a | bb | ccc | d | e
Result: a##de

Two-sum example:
values = [2, 7, 11], target = 9
At 2: complement is 7; remember 2 → index 0.
At 7: complement is 2; it is already in the map.
Answer: indices 0 and 1.
lesson.explanation: For run compression, one pointer marks the start of a run and another moves to its end. Every character belongs to exactly one run, so the total work is linear. For two-sum, the hash map describes values already visited. Looking up the complement before inserting the current value prevents using one index twice. A string builder or list of fragments avoids repeated expensive concatenation.
lesson.pitfall: A global character count loses order and cannot distinguish separated runs. A set alone loses indices when the output requires positions.
lesson.checkpoint: Explain the difference between a substring, a subsequence and a run. What should compression do to ababa?

lesson.title: Use a state you can explain
lesson.example:
Houses: [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
Best after each prefix: 2, 7, 11, 11, 12

best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + money[i])

Fixed window: [2, 1, 5, 1], k = 3
First sum: 8
Next sum: 8 - 2 + 1 = 7
lesson.explanation: The house-robber choice is exhaustive: either skip the current house, or take it and exclude its immediate neighbour. Only the previous two best totals are needed, so extra memory can stay constant. A fixed sliding window reuses the previous sum. Bracket matching uses a stack because the most recent opening bracket must be closed first.
lesson.pitfall: Do not initialize a maximum sum to zero when every valid sum may be negative. Do not overwrite a DP value before using its previous value.
lesson.checkpoint: Why does a greedy rule that always picks the next largest house fail on [2, 1, 1, 2]? Trace the two-state recurrence.

lesson.title: Think in rows before groups
lesson.example:
SELECT p.player_id, COUNT(r.id) AS paid_count
FROM player p
LEFT JOIN registration r
  ON p.player_id = r.player_id
 AND r.payment_status = 'Paid'
GROUP BY p.player_id
ORDER BY p.player_id;
lesson.explanation: The driving table is player because every player must appear. LEFT JOIN keeps a player with no paid registration, producing a row with null right-side values. COUNT(r.id) counts actual registrations and ignores that null. Moving the payment predicate into WHERE would remove zero-match players. Use HAVING when the condition is about a group total, such as at least three registrations.
lesson.pitfall: COUNT(*) counts the null-extended row, so it can report one instead of zero after a LEFT JOIN. Grouping only by a name can merge different people.
lesson.checkpoint: Write a query for players with no registrations. Explain why WHERE r.id IS NULL is useful after a LEFT JOIN.

lesson.title: Connect structure, presentation and behavior
lesson.explanation: HTML supplies semantic elements and stable selectors, CSS describes presentation, and JavaScript handles changes over time. Read the existing markup before writing a selector. Keep the state change separate from the event binding: attach listeners once, then update the relevant DOM. textContent displays user-entered text without interpreting it as HTML.
lesson.pitfall: An ID mismatch makes getElementById return null. Adding a new event listener on every render can make one click fire several times.

lesson.title: Model the component state
lesson.example:
Carousel with 3 slides:
next index = (current + 1) % 3
previous index = (current - 1 + 3) % 3

General circular normalization:
index = ((requested % total) + total) % total

Cart state:
{ productId: 12, unitPrice: 80, quantity: 3 }
line total = 80 × 3 = 240
lesson.explanation: A carousel needs one current index, then derives which slide and indicator are active. A cart needs distinct item identifiers and quantities; derive totals from state rather than repeatedly adding to the displayed text. For a chat widget, trim input, skip empty messages, append safe text, clear the field and scroll after the new message exists.
lesson.pitfall: String concatenation can turn 80 + 80 into 8080 when values came from input fields. Negative modulo differs across languages.
lesson.checkpoint: Write a checklist for first/last navigation, repeated cart additions, independent products, and blank messages. Run the checks after every change.

lesson.title: Make a compact fundamentals sheet
lesson.example:
Binary: 5 = 101, 3 = 011, 5 XOR 3 = 110 = 6
Absolute spreadsheet reference: $A$1
TCP: ordered, reliable byte delivery
DNS: names → resource records
IaaS: infrastructure; PaaS: managed platform; SaaS: finished application
Atomicity: all transaction changes commit, or none do
lesson.explanation: For pseudocode, track one variable table after each statement and state the language assumptions explicitly. For core CS, explain the purpose and trade-off of each mechanism: an index speeds some reads but adds write cost; threads share an address space but not their stacks; TLS secures transport but does not certify a business. For spreadsheets, distinguish relative references, exact lookup and conditional aggregation.
lesson.pitfall: Do not apply language-specific increment or signed-shift rules to ambiguous pseudocode without checking the prompt. Memorized acronyms are less useful than one concrete example.
lesson.checkpoint: Explain WHERE versus HAVING, TCP versus UDP, and PaaS versus SaaS without looking at notes. Then revisit the questions you missed.

lesson.title: Separate facts from assumptions
lesson.example:
All testers are engineers.
Some engineers are designers.

Guaranteed: all testers are engineers.
Not guaranteed: any tester is a designer.

STAR outline:
Situation → Task → Action you took → Result and lesson
lesson.explanation: For reasoning, ask whether a conclusion must follow, not whether it could be true. Use small diagrams or counterexamples when permitted by the real assessment. In communication, answer the question first, then support it with a short example. Workplace judgement practice should encourage ownership, collaboration and evidence, not teach candidates to pretend to have a particular personality.
lesson.pitfall: A percentage increase and the same percentage decrease do not cancel: 100 → 120 → 96. In a project story, distinguish your contribution from the team's overall work.
lesson.checkpoint: Record a one-minute project explanation and listen for clarity and repetition. Write a 100–150-word email with a specific request, neutral evidence and a polite next step.

lesson.title: Rehearse a decision process
lesson.example:
45-minute coding rehearsal:
0–5 min: read both prompts and inspect examples
5–22 min: complete one reliable solution
22–38 min: work on the second problem
38–45 min: edge cases, output format, final submission

Adjust this plan to the actual question difficulty.
lesson.explanation: A rehearsal tests pacing and recovery as well as knowledge. Before coding, identify the output contract and a plausible complexity target. A wrong answer is a useful clue: compare expected and actual output, reduce the failing example, and decide whether the issue is parsing, algorithm, state or formatting. Keep a short error log rather than merely counting attempts.
lesson.pitfall: Passing a sample does not prove correctness. Avoid changing several unrelated lines at once when debugging, and do not spend the entire round on one difficult idea.
lesson.checkpoint: Review one failed case and explain the fix without looking at the final code. Repeat the same pattern on a different input.

schedule.title: Rehearse the complete round

lesson.title: Turn review into a calm final rehearsal
lesson.example:
Exam-day check:
□ Official invitation and correct test link
□ Permitted ID and candidate details
□ Allowed language and environment requirements
□ Charger, connection, browser and system test
□ Time zone and reporting time
□ Quiet practice/review window and sufficient rest
lesson.explanation: Use the last day for retrieval and confidence in familiar skills. Re-solve a small set of previously missed problems without notes, explain the mistakes, then stop adding large new topics. Your actual invitation takes precedence over remembered campus reports. Interview preparation can cover problem solving, project architecture, CS fundamentals and teamwork without assuming exactly four panels.
lesson.pitfall: Do not mistake completing a checklist for a guaranteed outcome. Do not use this preparation site's AI tools or notes during a real assessment unless its rules explicitly permit them.
lesson.checkpoint: Can you outline your approach to an array problem, a grouped SQL query and a DOM event task? If not, choose one focused revision session rather than a new full syllabus.

lesson.title: A reliable first program
lesson.example:
Input: 6
2 5 4 7 8 9

Python:
values = [2, 5, 4, 7, 8, 9]
count = 0
for index, value in enumerate(values):
    if index % 2 == value % 2:
        count += 1
print(count)  # 6
lesson.explanation: An index describes a position, not a value. Enumerate supplies both. The counter means: how many matching positions have been seen so far. Before the loop it is zero; each iteration changes it only when the condition holds. This gives a simple correctness argument. For submitted problems, replace the demonstration array with input parsing and print only the answer.
lesson.pitfall: Do not assume values are positive or use one-based positions when a prompt specifies zero-based indices.
lesson.checkpoint: Can you explain what the counter represents after the first three iterations? Test a one-element array and an array containing negative odd values.

lesson.title: Scan once, keep the right state
lesson.example:
String: abbcccde
Runs: a | bb | ccc | d | e
Result: a##de

Two-sum example:
values = [2, 7, 11], target = 9
At 2: complement is 7; remember 2 → index 0.
At 7: complement is 2; it is already in the map.
Answer: indices 0 and 1.
lesson.explanation: For run compression, one pointer marks the start of a run and another moves to its end. Every character belongs to exactly one run, so the total work is linear. For two-sum, the hash map describes values already visited. Looking up the complement before inserting the current value prevents using one index twice. A string builder or list of fragments avoids repeated expensive concatenation.
lesson.pitfall: A global character count loses order and cannot distinguish separated runs. A set alone loses indices when the output requires positions.
lesson.checkpoint: Explain the difference between a substring, a subsequence and a run. What should compression do to ababa?

schedule.title: Think in states & algorithms · Learn

Read the worked example and trace it on paper or mentally.

lesson.title: Use a state you can explain
lesson.example:
Houses: [2, 7, 9, 3, 1]
Best after each prefix: 2, 7, 11, 11, 12

best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + money[i])

Fixed window: [2, 1, 5, 1], k = 3
First sum: 8
Next sum: 8 - 2 + 1 = 7
lesson.explanation: The house-robber choice is exhaustive: either skip the current house, or take it and exclude its immediate neighbour. Only the previous two best totals are needed, so extra memory can stay constant. A fixed sliding window reuses the previous sum. Bracket matching uses a stack because the most recent opening bracket must be closed first.
lesson.pitfall: Do not initialize a maximum sum to zero when every valid sum may be negative. Do not overwrite a DP value before using its previous value.
lesson.checkpoint: Why does a greedy rule that always picks the next largest house fail on [2, 1, 1, 2]? Trace the two-state recurrence.

lesson.title: Think in rows before groups
lesson.example:
SELECT p.player_id, COUNT(r.id) AS paid_count
FROM player p
LEFT JOIN registration r
  ON p.player_id = r.player_id
 AND r.payment_status = 'Paid'
GROUP BY p.player_id
ORDER BY p.player_id;
lesson.explanation: The driving table is player because every player must appear. LEFT JOIN keeps a player with no paid registration, producing a row with null right-side values. COUNT(r.id) counts actual registrations and ignores that null. Moving the payment predicate into WHERE would remove zero-match players. Use HAVING when the condition is about a group total, such as at least three registrations.
lesson.pitfall: COUNT(*) counts the null-extended row, so it can report one instead of zero after a LEFT JOIN. Grouping only by a name can merge different people.
lesson.checkpoint: Write a query for players with no registrations. Explain why WHERE r.id IS NULL is useful after a LEFT JOIN.

lesson.title: Model the component state
lesson.example:
Carousel with 3 slides:
next index = (current + 1) % 3
previous index = (current - 1 + 3) % 3

General circular normalization:
index = ((requested % total) + total) % total

Cart state:
{ productId: 12, unitPrice: 80, quantity: 3 }
line total = 80 × 3 = 240
lesson.explanation: A carousel needs one current index, then derives which slide and indicator are active. A cart needs distinct item identifiers and quantities; derive totals from state rather than repeatedly adding to the displayed text. For a chat widget, trim input, skip empty messages, append safe text, clear the field and scroll after the new message exists.
lesson.pitfall: String concatenation can turn 80 + 80 into 8080 when values came from input fields. Negative modulo differs across languages.
lesson.checkpoint: Write a checklist for first/last navigation, repeated cart additions, independent products, and blank messages. Run the checks after every change.

lesson.title: Make a compact fundamentals sheet
lesson.example:
Binary: 5 = 101, 3 = 011, 5 XOR 3 = 110 = 6
Absolute spreadsheet reference: $A$1
TCP: ordered, reliable byte delivery
DNS: names → resource records
IaaS: infrastructure; PaaS: managed platform; SaaS: finished application
Atomicity: all transaction changes commit, or none do
lesson.explanation: For pseudocode, track one variable table after each statement and state the language assumptions explicitly. For core CS, explain the purpose and trade-off of each mechanism: an index speeds some reads but adds write cost; threads share an address space but not their stacks; TLS secures transport but does not certify a business. For spreadsheets, distinguish relative references, exact lookup and conditional aggregation.
lesson.pitfall: Do not apply language-specific increment or signed-shift rules to ambiguous pseudocode without checking the prompt. Memorized acronyms are less useful than one concrete example.
lesson.checkpoint: Explain WHERE versus HAVING, TCP versus UDP, and PaaS versus SaaS without looking at notes. Then revisit the questions you missed.

lesson.pitfall: Do not apply language-specific increment or signed-shift rules to ambiguous pseudocode without checking the prompt. Memorized acronyms are less useful than one concrete example.
lesson.checkpoint: Explain WHERE versus HAVING, TCP versus UDP, and PaaS versus SaaS without looking at notes. Then revisit the questions you missed.

lesson.title: Rehearse a decision process
lesson.example:
45-minute coding rehearsal:
0–5 min: read both prompts and inspect examples
5–22 min: complete one reliable solution
22–38 min: work on the second problem
38–45 min: edge cases, output format, final submission

Adjust this plan to the actual question difficulty.
lesson.explanation: A rehearsal tests pacing and recovery as well as knowledge. Before coding, identify the output contract and a plausible complexity target. A wrong answer is a useful clue: compare expected and actual output, reduce the failing example, and decide whether the issue is parsing, algorithm, state or formatting. Keep a short error log rather than merely counting attempts.
lesson.pitfall: Passing a sample does not prove correctness. Avoid changing several unrelated lines at once when debugging, and do not spend the entire round on one difficult idea.
lesson.checkpoint: Review one failed case and explain the fix without looking at the final code. Repeat the same pattern on a different input.

lesson.title: Turn review into a calm final rehearsal
lesson.example:
Exam-day check:
□ Official invitation and correct test link
□ Permitted ID and candidate details
□ Allowed language and environment requirements
□ Charger, connection, browser and system test
□ Time zone and reporting time
□ Quiet practice/review window and sufficient rest
lesson.explanation: Use the last day for retrieval and confidence in familiar skills. Re-solve a small set of previously missed problems without notes, explain the mistakes, then stop adding large new topics. Your actual invitation takes precedence over remembered campus reports. Interview preparation can cover problem solving, project architecture, CS fundamentals and teamwork without assuming exactly four panels.
lesson.pitfall: Do not mistake completing a checklist for a guaranteed outcome. Do not use this preparation site's AI tools or notes during a real assessment unless its rules explicitly permit them.
lesson.checkpoint: Can you outline your approach to an array problem, a grouped SQL query and a DOM event task? If not, choose one focused revision session rather than a new full syllabus.
